summary: Small, cold-loving estuary cod relative that turns into a genuine winter ice-fishing target in a few NB/NS estuaries — a real regional tradition worth knowing, alongside its usual role as a bonus catch on flounder gear the rest of the year.

sections.heading: Know the Fish
sections.body_md:
Atlantic tomcod (*Microgadus tomcod*) are small, bottom-oriented members of the cod family, maxing out around 15 cm/6 in — a true dwarf relative of Atlantic cod, not a juvenile of that species (they're a distinct species entirely). Look for the classic small-cod body shape: three dorsal fins, two anal fins, and a small barbel under the chin, but scaled down to a fraction of Atlantic cod's size. In the Mi'kmaq language they're known as *punamu*; the common nickname "frostfish" across their range comes directly from their habit of running upriver to spawn in the dead of winter, in January, when almost nothing else is active.

Tomcod are an estuarine species tolerant of a wide range of salinity and temperature, and unlike most fish in this guide they're at their most active and most targeted during the coldest part of the year.

sections.heading: The Winter Ice-Fishing Tradition
sections.body_md:
Tomcod support a genuine, longstanding **winter estuary fishery** in Nova Scotia that's distinct from anything else in this guide — most saltwater species here are summer/fall targets, but tomcod peak in January.

- The **Shubenacadie River** estuary is the best-documented tomcod water in the region: fishers work the snow-covered banks and ice in winter, historically using **wire traps** set in the icy water to catch fish as they run upriver to spawn.
- This lines up with the species' "frostfish" nickname and its January spawning run — tomcod are one of the only fish actively targeted through the ice in tidal/estuary settings in this region, as opposed to freshwater lake ice fishing for trout and other species.
- The tradition has deep Indigenous roots (the Mi'kmaq name *punamu* reflects long-standing harvest of this species) and continues today; the Apoqnmatulti'k research project, which pairs Western science with Indigenous and local knowledge holders, currently monitors tomcod movements and habitat in Nova Scotia, underlining how significant the species still is culturally and ecologically.
- Elsewhere in the wider Gulf of St. Lawrence region, tomcod are also taken through the ice in good numbers, reinforcing that this is a real, geographically broad winter tradition, not a one-river curiosity.

sections.heading: When to Go
sections.body_md: Two distinct windows: **January**, during the spawning run, is peak season for the dedicated winter/ice fishery described above, especially in known estuaries like the Shubenacadie. Outside that window, tomcod are present in deeper estuary channels through the open-water season and are commonly caught **incidentally** while targeting winter flounder with the same bottom rigs — worth knowing so you don't mistake a bonus tomcod for something else on your flounder line.

sections.heading: Where to Find Them
sections.body_md:
- **NS:** The **Shubenacadie River** estuary is the signature winter tomcod water in this region. Beyond that, tomcod are broadly present along Nova Scotia's estuaries wherever winter flounder are also found.
- **NB:** Deeper estuary channels of the **Cocagne and Shediac River** systems hold tomcod, typically encountered as bycatch on flounder gear rather than targeted directly.
- **PEI:** The Boughton Bay/Three Rivers estuary similarly holds tomcod alongside winter flounder, again mostly as an incidental catch on the same gear.

In any of these systems, deeper estuary channels and the same soft-bottom areas that hold winter flounder are the right water.

sections.heading: Gear
sections.body_md:
| Item | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Open-water rod | Same light spinning setup used for winter flounder — 6-6'6" ML rod, light line. |
| Rig | Hi-lo bottom rig baited with small strips of bait, fished on or near bottom. |
| Ice fishing (traditional) | Historically, wire traps set through the ice at the river mouth during the January run — a distinct method from typical hook-and-line ice fishing gear used for freshwater species. |
| Bait | Small strips of clam, worm, or other bottom bait. |

sections.heading: Technique
sections.body_md:
**Open-water/incidental (spring-fall):**
1. Fish the same hi-lo bottom rig used for winter flounder in deeper estuary channels.
2. Slow retrieve with frequent pauses on bottom — tomcod bite is subtle, similar to flounder.
3. Treat any tomcod caught this way as a bonus, not a dedicated target.

**Winter run (January, e.g. Shubenacadie):**
1. Target the estuary/river mouth during the spawning push in January.
2. Traditional method uses wire traps set in the ice; modern anglers can also still-fish with small baited hooks near bottom through a hole if ice conditions allow safe access.
3. Always confirm ice safety and access locally before attempting any ice fishing — conditions vary year to year and estuary ice is less predictable than a closed freshwater lake.

sections.heading: Handling & Table Notes
sections.body_md: Tomcod are a traditional food fish in this region, particularly tied to the winter run — hence the Hakai Magazine framing of tomcod as a fish that "brings everyone to the table." Small size means they're typically cooked whole or lightly cleaned rather than filleted. Handle gently if releasing; being a small, delicate-mouthed fish, they don't tolerate rough handling well.

sources.label: Hakai Magazine, Tomcod Brings Everyone to the Table

sections.heading: Conservation Notes
sections.body_md: No specific at-risk status turned up for Atlantic tomcod in this region. DFO's Maritimes Region recreational fisheries materials list tomcod distinct from Atlantic cod (i.e., tomcod aren't subject to Atlantic cod's stricter conservation rules), and no dedicated bag limit turned up in current notices — fish conservatively regardless, particularly given the cultural and ecological significance of the winter spawning run described above.
